problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-1,0).$ Find the polar coordinates of $P.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$

examples.knowledge_point: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates for a Point on an Axis
examples.problem: Express the Cartesian point $P (0,-7)$ in polar coordinates.
examples.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		r &= \sqrt{0^2 + (-7)^2}\
		&= \sqrt{7^2}\
		&= 7
	}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies on the negative half of the $y$-axis, we have $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}.$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $\left(7, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right).$

feedback.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(-2a,a),$ where $a$ is a positive real number. What are the polar coordinates of $P?$  Round your answer to the nearest tenth where appropriate.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2a)^{2}+{a}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{a}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\text{ }\,a.\end{aligned}
$$

For the reference angle, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{-2a})| \\  & =|-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{2})| \\  & ≈0.463\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies in the second quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $\pi ,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & ≈\pi -0.463\,6 \\  & ≈2.7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are  $(\sqrt{5}\text{ }\,a,2.7).$
